trend_source: A 22-year-old realtor's 'what I made vs what I spent in August' video, walking through every income stream and every expense line, has 831.7k views, 107.2k likes and 6.4k shares on TikTok.
title: What I earned vs what I spent last month, as a commission earner in Singapore
hooks: I tracked every dollar I earned and spent in August. One line on the spending side genuinely surprised me.
Commission months are never the same, so here is exactly what came in and what went out last month.
Most people know their salary. Almost nobody knows what they actually spent last month. Here is mine.
talking_points: List every income source for the month, including any side income, and say the total out loud
Walk through the fixed costs first (housing loan or rent, transport, insurance premiums), then the variable spending
Point out the one category that crept up without you noticing
If part of your income is commission or freelance, set money aside for income tax, because nothing is deducted each month like a salary
cta: Comment TRACKER and I will send you the simple earned-vs-spent sheet I use every month.
why_it_works: Money transparency videos pull huge numbers because viewers compare themselves line by line. An advisor showing their own real breakdown builds trust without selling anything.
how_to_film: Talking head or a screen recording of a simple sheet. Say the income total in the first 3 seconds, then go line by line with each amount on screen. Keep it under 90 seconds.
author: @leila_tuck

trend_source: A 50-second 'put your money in this account if...' video listing where each dollar should go every month has 330.1k views, 22.4k likes and 5.4k shares on TikTok. The original covers US accounts.
title: Where your money should go every month, the Singapore version
hooks: Put your money in an emergency fund first if one surprise bill would send you straight to your credit card.
Here is where every dollar of my pay goes each month, and why almost none of it sits in a normal savings account.
If all your money is in one savings account, this is the Singapore version of where it should go instead.
talking_points: Emergency fund first: 3 to 6 months of expenses in a high-interest savings account you can reach quickly
Basic protection next: a hospitalisation plan and enough cover that one bad diagnosis does not wipe out your savings
SRS contributions and CPF cash top-ups can lower your income tax up to the yearly limits, so check the current caps before topping up
Then invest regularly for the long term, and keep only one to two months of spending in your everyday account
cta: Save this and send it to the friend who keeps everything in one bank account.
why_it_works: The rapid 'put your money here if' format is proven and easy to follow, and swapping US accounts for Singapore ones makes it genuinely useful locally.
how_to_film: Fast talking head, one account per cut, each account name as on-screen text. Open with the first 'put your money here if' line, no intro.
author: @the.finance.engineer

trend_source: A 23-year-old's 'first payday routine of September' video, budgeting one paycheck line by line while paying down debt, has 57.2k views and 5.4k likes on TikTok.
title: My payday routine while paying off a credit card
hooks: Payday hit and within ten minutes most of it already had somewhere to go. Here is my routine.
This is exactly what I do the day my pay comes in, in the order I do it.
If your pay disappears by the 10th, try doing these four things on payday instead.
talking_points: Start from your take-home pay after CPF, because that is the real number you are budgeting
Pay the fixed bills and move your savings on payday itself, before any spending
Pay more than the minimum on any credit card balance, since card interest in Singapore is usually well above 20% a year
Cancel or pause one subscription a month and put that amount towards the card
cta: Comment PAYDAY and I will send you my payday checklist.
why_it_works: Payday routine videos feel honest and repeatable, and the debt angle gives an advisor a natural, non-salesy reason to talk about cash flow.
how_to_film: Screen record your banking app with balances blurred, or talk to camera with each step as a caption. Start with the pay landing and go step by step in under 60 seconds.
author: @dejamonea

trend_source: A 'how I would budget a $60K salary' video arguing the 50/30/20 rule no longer works, with a line-by-line monthly split, has 53.1k views, 2.3k likes and 232 comments on TikTok.
title: The 50/30/20 rule does not fit a $4,000 take-home in Singapore, so try this
hooks: The 50/30/20 rule stopped working the moment rent and transport went up. Here is the split I would use now.
If you take home about $4,000 a month in Singapore, this is how I would split it.
Budgeting rules from ten years ago do not survive today's prices, so here is a realistic version.
talking_points: Work from take-home pay after CPF, and accept that needs can honestly take 60 to 70% right now
Build a 3 to 6 month emergency fund before investing anything
Keep a small, guilt-free wants budget so the plan actually lasts
Once the emergency fund is done, redirect that same monthly amount into long-term investing and any protection gaps
cta: Comment BUDGET and I will send you the split as a simple sheet.

author: @joyeeyang0

trend_source: A 40-year-old mum and business owner's 'unhinged things I am doing to 10x my income' video (failing publicly, trying weird ideas, aiming absurdly high) has 16.3k views, 1.8k likes and 333 comments on TikTok.
title: Before you chase a bigger income, lock in these three things
hooks: Everyone is trying to 10x their income this year. Almost nobody is protecting the income they already have.
I love the side hustle energy online, but here is what I would sort out before chasing more money.
If you are building a second income, do these three boring things first so one bad month does not undo it.
talking_points: Keep a separate emergency fund so a slow month in the new venture does not become credit card debt
Set aside money for tax on side income, since nothing is deducted for you
Your ability to earn is your biggest asset, so check what happens to your income if illness or injury stops you working
Then go for it: aim high, try the weird idea, and review your plan every few months
cta: What side income are you working on? Tell me in the comments.
why_it_works: Ambition content gets strong comment engagement, and the protect-before-you-grow angle lets an advisor join in without killing the energy.

author: @lindseyyyymartin

trend_source: A 'here is how I am investing $10,000 in 2026' video splitting the money across different funds has 13.9k views and 508 comments on TikTok, an unusually high comment rate for its views.
title: Before you invest your first $10,000, check these three things
hooks: Everyone online is telling you where to put $10,000. Nobody is asking whether you are ready to invest it.
Before you put $10,000 into anything, answer these three questions first.
I get asked how to invest the first $10k a lot. My answer always starts somewhere else.
talking_points: Do you have 3 to 6 months of expenses saved separately, so you never have to sell investments in an emergency
Are you protected, so a hospital bill or a health scare does not force you to cash out
When will you need this money? Money for a home in two years should not be invested like money for retirement in thirty
Once those are sorted, spreading money across different investments is usually safer than putting it all in one place
cta: Comment READY and I will send you the three-question checklist.
why_it_works: Investing split videos get lots of comments, and an advisor can join the conversation responsibly by focusing on readiness instead of naming funds.
how_to_film: Hold up a sticky note with $10,000 on it, then flip three cards, one question each. Keep it under 45 seconds.
author: @calltoleap

trend_source: A 31-year-old tech worker sharing her seven-figure portfolio by percentage, including 31% in her employer's company stock, has 42.4k views and 1.3k likes on TikTok.
title: If you work in tech, your company shares might be your biggest risk
hooks: A lot of people in tech have their job and a big chunk of their savings tied to the same company.
If your RSUs are the biggest thing in your portfolio, watch this before your next vesting date.
Your salary, your bonus and your shares all depend on one company. That is worth thinking about.
talking_points: Add up what percentage of your net worth sits in your employer's shares, including unvested ones
If the company has a bad year, your job, bonus and shares can all fall at the same time
Decide in advance what you will do at each vesting date, so emotions do not decide for you
Make sure your emergency fund and protection do not depend on those shares
cta: Save this for your next vesting date.
why_it_works: Portfolio transparency videos draw curious viewers, and concentration risk is a real, specific issue for Singapore's tech workers that an advisor can explain without making market calls.
how_to_film: Talking head with a simple pie chart. Open on the pie with the company stock slice highlighted.
author: @triciasfu

trend_source: A 55-second 'two signs you are doing financially well even if it does not feel like it' video has 34.5k views, 941 likes and 81 comments on TikTok.
title: Two signs you are doing better with money than you think
hooks: You might be doing better financially than you feel, especially if these two things are true.
If you feel behind your friends with money, check these two signs first.
Nobody posts their emergency fund on Instagram, which is exactly why you feel behind.
talking_points: Sign one: you could cover a few months of expenses without borrowing, which many people cannot
Real wealth is mostly invisible, like savings, CPF balances and protection, not the car or the renovation
Sign two: you have stopped measuring yourself against friends' salaries and lifestyles
Your plan only has to fit your own goals and timeline, not anyone else's
cta: Which of these two signs is true for you? Tell me below.
why_it_works: Reassurance content spreads because people send it to friends who feel behind, and it lets an advisor talk about emergency funds without fear tactics.

trend_source: A Singapore street interview asking students what salary they want, and whether $5,000 or $7,000 to $8,000 a month is enough for a comfortable life, has 13.6k views on Instagram, about 5.5 times the creator's usual reach.
title: Is $5,000 a month enough in Singapore? It depends on three things
hooks: Ask any fresh grad and they will say $7,000 to $8,000 a month is the dream. Here is what it actually has to cover.
Is $5,000 a month enough to live comfortably in Singapore? The honest answer depends on three things.
Everyone has a number for their dream salary. Almost nobody has a number for their dream life.
talking_points: Take-home pay after CPF is what you actually live on, so a $5,000 salary means less in your pocket each month
The big swing factors are housing, whether you plan to have kids, and how much you want to travel
Pick the lifestyle first, price it out, then work backwards to the income and savings you need
Protect the plan along the way: emergency fund first, then basic cover so one setback does not reset you to zero
cta: What monthly salary do you think is enough in Singapore today? Drop your number below.
why_it_works: Salary number debates are relatable and invite everyone to comment their own figure, and turning that number into a lifestyle plan is exactly an advisor's lane.
how_to_film: Street-interview style or talking head with the salary numbers as big on-screen text. Say the dream salary figure in the first line.
author: @juliusyipp

trend_source: A Singapore financial adviser explaining why he bought a Continental car three years into his career, and arguing that how you reward yourself is personal preference, has 11.7k views on Instagram, about 5.4 times his usual reach.
title: Want the nice car as a reward? Do the math first so it stays guilt-free
hooks: I am not here to judge your dream car. I just want you to know what it really costs before you sign.
Rewarding yourself after years of hard work is fine. Here is how to make sure the reward does not become a regret.
In Singapore a car is rarely just a car payment, and that is where the reward gets expensive.
talking_points: Count the full monthly cost, not just the instalment: COE, loan interest, insurance, road tax, parking, petrol and servicing
Compare it honestly against your real alternative, whether that is Grab, public transport or a cheaper model
Decide on the reward only after this month's emergency fund and savings are already done
If the car is for work, keep a buffer in case your income dips while the loan payments continue
cta: Save this before you visit the showroom.
why_it_works: Big purchase debates like Conti versus Japanese cars get people talking, and a no-judgement, do-the-math angle builds trust instead of lecturing.
how_to_film: Talking head, in or beside a car if you can. Put each cost line on screen as you say it and show the monthly total at the end.
author: @seantalkssg

trend_source: A Singapore parent explaining why she chose her own retirement over fully funding her kids' university, and her plan to invest the government baby bonus cash instead of letting it sit, has 22.8k views on Instagram, about 3.9 times the creator's usual reach.
title: Retirement first or your kid's uni fund first? Here is how I would think about it
hooks: Saving for my retirement before my kid's university fund sounds selfish. Here is why it might be the kinder choice.
If you can only fully fund one, your retirement or your child's university, which do you pick?
Your kids can borrow for university. Nobody lends you money for retirement.
talking_points: An underfunded retirement often becomes your children's burden later, so securing it first can protect them too
Baby bonus cash that sits idle for 18 years tends to lose ground to rising university fees
Putting those payouts to work early for the long term gives them more time to grow, matched to your family's comfort with risk
Check the latest Baby Bonus and CDA amounts on the official government site before you plan around them
cta: Retirement first or uni fund first? Tell me which you would pick.
why_it_works: It is a genuine parenting dilemma with a slightly controversial answer, which drives comments, and it sits squarely in an advisor's expertise.
how_to_film: Calm, personal talking head. Open with the dilemma as on-screen text, then share your view.

trend_source: A finance creator's 'the person who can afford to buy but rents on purpose' video, showing how much of a mortgage's first 10 years goes to interest instead of equity, has 96.6k views and 2k likes on Instagram, about 3 times his usual reach. The numbers in the original are US ones.
title: Before you upgrade your home, check how much of your payments is just interest
hooks: In the first years of a big home loan, a lot of every payment is interest, not ownership. Here is how to check yours.
Upgrading to a bigger place? Look at how much of your first ten years of payments actually becomes equity.
Renting is not always throwing money away, and buying is not always building wealth. It depends on the math.
talking_points: Ask your bank for the loan's repayment schedule and see how much of the first 10 years goes to interest versus principal
Add the costs that build no equity at all: property tax, insurance, maintenance or condo fees, and renovation
A lower interest rate or a shorter loan changes the picture a lot, so compare the options side by side
Whatever you choose, keep your emergency fund and protection separate from the house, because the loan does not pause if your income does
cta: Save this before your next property viewing.
why_it_works: Contrarian money takes like renting on purpose get shared and argued about, and walking through interest versus equity is useful for anyone in Singapore thinking about upgrading.
how_to_film: Talking head with a simple bar showing interest versus principal over 10 years. Open with the contrarian line.
author: @humphreytalks
